Tantras
------------------------------------------
1. Introduction
It is seen that every major religion of the world has a founder, a scripture and a church. हिन्दुइस्म् is the solitary exception to this general pattern. It does not have a single founder or a single book or a single church, though in it great reli-gious leaders, religious books and religious monasteries or organisations are legion.
Although the वेदस् have been accepted as the basic scriptures by most of the sects, cults and groups of हिन्दुइस्म्, a number of other religio-philosophical works have appeared over the centuries, many of which have occupied cardinal positions in their cults or sects. The आगमस् and the तन्त्रस् form an important category of literature among these.
Originally, the word ‘tantra’ seems to have meant any science or body of knowledge. Gradually, however, it got restricted to a particular class of literature, a literature primarily devoted to the cult of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् and containing an amalgam of religion, philosophy, esoteric and occult rites, अस्त्रोनोम्य्, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, medicine and prognostications. In this respect, the तन्त्रस् resemble the पुराणस्. Etymologically the word is derived from its two constituents—‘tan,’ to spread; ‘trai,’ to protect—and is supposed to mean any work that spreads or dilates upon many matters like tattvas (fundamental principles) and mantras (sacred words and syllables) and through that knowledge affords protection to the votaries.
Whether the तन्त्रस् have accepted the authority of the वेदस् and hence their subservience to them, or, have furrowed their own parallel and independent path, is a moot point. If the stress on मोक्ष (freedom from transmigratory existence) as also the place of honour accorded to the वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas (duties based on castes and stations in life) bespeaks of their allegiance to the वेदस्, other practices like the pañca-makāras or शवसाधना (to be explained later) smack of their close association with an aboriginal, non-Vedic, society. It may, perhaps, be safer to assume that though they might have originated as a parallel tradition distancing themselves from the Vedic tradition, later teachers of the schools of tantra might have endeavoured to bring them much closer to the latter, if not integrate them into it.
Tāntric Literature
According to the tāntric texts, the तन्त्रस् are innumerable. Sometimes they are stated to be 64. The number however, varies from scripture to scripture.
There are several ways of classifying the tāntric texts. According to one tradition, the works in which सदाशिव speaks to the देवी are called ‘āgamas’ and those in which the देवी speaks to सदाशिव or महेश्वर, are named as ‘nigamas.’ As per another grouping, they are: dakṣiṇa, vāma and madhyama. A third method groups them into three: दिव्य, कौल and vāma.
A selected list of works that have been printed तन्त्रस् are still lying in the libraries of Oriental Institutes and other institutions.">1, confining it only to the देवी-cult, may now be given:
Īśāna-gurudeva-paddhati
Kāmakalāvilāsa

Sometimes, mention is also made of two types of तन्त्रस्, the Yāmala and the डामर.
The Yāmala group gets its name because it contains the secret conversations between the deity and his consort, who form the couple (yāmala = united, couple). ‘Ḍāmara’ means a goblin, an attendant of शिव. It also means ‘wonder’. Hence that class of तन्त्रस् attributed to शिव and containing wondrous teachings is ‘Ḍāmaratantra’.
The Yāmalatantras are:
Brahmayāmala, Viṣṇuyāmala,
Rudrayāmala, Lakṣmīyāmala,
Umāyāmala, Skandayāmala,
Gaṇeśayāmala and Ādityayāmala.
The Ḍāmaratantras are:
Yogaḍāmara, Śivaḍāmara,
Durgāḍāmara, Sārasvataḍāmara,
Brahmaḍāmara and Gandharvaḍāmara.
There are a good number of other तन्त्रस् also like Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa and Guhyasamāja-tantra belonging to the Buddhist tradition.
3. Contents of the तन्त्रस् in Brief
Though there are various kinds of आगमस् and तन्त्रस्, certain features are common to them all. They avow allegiance to the वेदस्, and even claim to interpret them to the current age. However, unlike the वेदस्, their doors are open to all, irrespective of caste or sex.
The subjects generally dealt with by them are classed under four pādas or steps. They are: Jñānapāda, Yogapāda, Kriyāpāda and Caryāpāda.
The Jñānapāda gives the philosophy or the metaphysics upon which the तन्त्रस् are based. It is a combination of the Vedāntic and the Sāṅkhyan principles.
The Yogapāda deals with the sādhanās or spiritual disciplines that help an individual aspirant to attain union with the Supreme Self, which is the final goal of life.
Since an individual is a part and parcel of the society and since his spiritual progress is closely allied with that of the society, the तन्त्रस् give to the society also a way of life, a religion, so that both the individual and the society can progress in harmony with each other. Towards this end, the तन्त्रस् provide the institution of community worship as in a temple or through a याग (sacrifice) or through the sacred spots of पिल्ग्रिमगे. These are the topics described in the Kriyāpāda, the third of the series of the four pādas.
Caryāpāda, the last, expounds the rituals and the modes of sādhanās needed in an individual’s life. A code of conduct is also given for the benefit of the tyro as well as the adept.
A good number of other topics are also dealt with, which may be summarised as follows: authenticity of the आगमस् and the तन्त्रस् based on the वेदस्; च्रेअतिओन् of the world; manifestation of वैखरी-vāk or the spoken word; on the letters of the alphabet; various rites connected with दीक्षा or initiation like the Vāstuyāga; categories of दीक्षा; on होम (fire ritual); various mantras connected with various deities of the Hindu pantheon like सरस्वती, Śrī or लक्ष्मी, भुवनेश्वरी, दुर्गा, विष्णु, गणपति, शिव and so on; yantras or geometrical configurations associated with those deities; yogic practices including the descriptions of कुण्डलिनी and the various चक्रस् or psychic centres and so on.
4. Philosophy of the Tantras
The philosophy of the तन्त्रस् seems to be an amalgamation and modification of the principles propounded by the Sāṅkhya and the Vedānta systems. The प्रकृति of Sāṅkhya is material and insentient in nature. The māyā of Vedānta, especially of the Advaita Vedānta, is an ‘entity’ that defies all descriptions. However, the शक्ति of the तन्त्रस् is a very real power of शिव, nay, शिव himself in his dynamic aspect. All other qualities that are predicated for प्रकृति-māyā like its being triguṇātmikā (comprising the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्) and the उपादानकारण (material cause) of the world, hold good for the शक्ति of the तन्त्रस् also.
The ultimate Reality is one and only one. It is शिव or शक्ति or शिव-शक्ति and is (‘saṁvit’) of the nature of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. The relationship between शिव and शक्ति is like that of fire and its burning power or the word and its meaning. They are two in one or one in two, always inseparable. In the inactive state it is शिव and in the active state it is शक्ति. The former is also called Nirguṇa-परमेश्वर (the Lord without attributes) wherein the शक्ति is inherent and dormant. When this शक्ति starts awakening, परमेश्वर becomes ‘Saguṇa.’ The first evolute of the process of च्रेअतिओन् is शक्ति. From शक्ति proceeds पर-नाद (the unmanifest sound or vibration which gives rise to पर-बिन्दु, the higher बिन्दु or point). From it proceed the apara-बिन्दु (lower बिन्दु or point, identified with the शिव-principle), the बीज (identified with the शक्ति-principle) and the apara-नाद (the lower sound or vibration) considered as the union of the शिव and the शक्ति principles.
From बीज or शक्ति (also called शब्द-brahma, पराशक्ति or Paradevatā) proceed the 23 tattvas or cosmic principles, viz., महत्, अहङ्कार, the ten इन्द्रियस् and the मिन्द्, the five subtle elements and the five gross elements like the earth, water etc. Together with शक्ति, they are 24.
From the apara-बिन्दु, identified with शिव, proceed the five deities viz., सदाशिव, ईशान, रुद्र, विष्णु and ब्रह्मा. By adding seven more principles like पुरुष (the individual सोउल्) and kāla (time), the total number of tattvas is raised to 36.
In the human body, शक्ति resides as the कुण्डलिनी, the power resembling a coiled serpent at the मूलाधार-चक्र, situated at the base of the spine. When roused through proper sādhanās or spiritual exercises, it rises through five more चक्रस् like the स्वाधिष्ठान and the anāhata, and, finally reaches the सहस्रार in the crown of the head, resembling a lotus of a thousand petals. there it merges with शिव, resulting in मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् for that individual self.
The जीव or the individual सोउल् is none other than शिव himself, with his freedom covered over or limited by अविद्या or nescience, also called āṇava-मल, the impurity that makes him appear small. Through spiritual disciplines, the most important aspect of which is upāsanā or worship and meditation, on शक्ति as देवी or Divine मोथेर्, he is liberated, attaining unity with the

. Sādhanās as Depicted in the Tantras
As in the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, in the तन्त्रस् also, मोक्ष, or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence, is the ultimate goal of life. The तन्त्रस् have evolved an elaborate system of sādhanās or spiritual practices that cover all aspects of the human personality and life. Only a brief résumé can be attempted here.
GURU
The तन्त्रस् categorically assert the need for taking दीक्षा or initiation from a competent गुरु or teacher before starting one’s spiritual sādhanās.
A competent गुरु must be a person of pure parentage and great self-control. He should know the true meaning and essence of the scriptures—the वेदस्, the आगमस् and related scriptures. He should be an adept in पूजा (worship), होम (pouring oblations into a duly consecrated fire), ध्यान (meditation) and जप (repetition of the divine name). A peaceful disposition and a thorough knowledge of योग are also necessary.
The तन्त्रस् also warn against accepting false gurus, who feign erudition and holiness, but are motivated by greed and baser instincts.
ŚIṢYA
The शिष्य or the disciple too must possess certain minimum characteristics which will entitle him to spiritual life.
He must be guileless, must aspire after the पुरुषार्थस् (goals of human existence) and be fairly well-read in the वेदस्. He should be self-controlled and intelligent enough to understand the teachings of the गुरु and the scriptures. He should be devoted to his parents, discharge his duties well and avoid all pride of birth or wealth or learning. He must be obedient to the गुरु and be prepared to sacrifice everything for his sake.
The तन्त्रस् declare that the गुरु must test a person before accepting him as a disciple and vice versa.
IṢṬADEVATĀ
Though God the Supreme is one without a second, he can and does manifest himself through various forms and emanations, all of which are non-different from him, even as sugar-dolls are all sugar only. The particular form a sādhaka or a votary chooses is his ‘iṣṭadevatā,’ ‘the deity dear to him’. He chooses that form for purposes of meditation and worship. The तन्त्रस् advocate meditation on and worship of these forms of God since it is much easier for an average human being, than contemplating on the Absolute without name and form.
Each of these देवतास् has a मन्त्र or even several mantras or word-symbols, which have to be ceremonially received in दीक्षा or initiation from a qualified गुरु.
DĪKṢĀ
Dīkṣā or initiation into spiritual life is so called because it destroys (kṣi = to destroy) the sins of the disciple and gives (dā = to give) knowledge to him. It should be given on a day and time considered to be holy as per the Hindu calendars. Days of eclipses—especially of the moon—are deemed to be extremely holy.
Several varieties of दीक्षा are enumerated in the tāntric works. One of the more well-known categorisations is as follows: kriyāvatī, varṇamayī, kalāvatī and vedhamayī. The kriyāvatī दीक्षा involves the performance of many rituals by the गुरु. In varṇamayī दीक्षा, the गुरु infuses the spirit of the varṇas or letters of the alphabet which are associated with शक्ति or देवी, in the different parts of the disciple’s body. In the kalāvatī दीक्षा the गुरु locates the existence of kalās or powers of the पञ्चभूतस् like nivṛttikalā or vidyākalā, in the body of the disciple, meditates on them and anoints him. In the vedhamayī दीक्षा, the गुरु initiates the disciple only by the power of his thought.
Sometimes three more varieties are added: sparśadīkṣā (rousing the spiritual चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् by sparśa or touch), vāgdīkṣā (same by uttering the मन्त्र into the ear of the disciple) and dṛgdīkṣā or चाक्षुषी दीक्षा (arousal of spiritual चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् by looking intently at the disciple).
Dīkṣā, in a more technical sense, involves a number of rituals like the worship of the वास्तुपुरुष (Cosmic Being) and बलि or sacrifice as also अभिषेक done by sprinkling holy water on the disciple.
Its simplest form is ‘upadeśa,’ giving the मन्त्र as also certain rules and guidance.
MANTRA
The central part of दीक्षा or upadeśa is the imparting of the मन्त्र or the divine word by the गुरु to the disciple. Etymologically, the word means that which protects (tra = to protect) the person who reflects (man = to reflect) upon it. ‘Protection’ in the spiritual sense means protecting from सṁसार or transmigratory existence by giving मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. The mantras may have their source in the वेदस् or the पुराणस् or the तन्त्रस्. Since the last group of works deals primarily with the mantras, it is called as ‘mantraśāstra’ or ‘mantravidyā’.
A मन्त्र, according to the तन्त्रस्, is not just a letter of the alphabet or a combination of such letters into a word or a sentence signifying a particular object. It is the sound symbol embodying the form, the power and the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the supreme ब्रह्मन् or its manifestations.
Before च्रेअतिओन्, ब्रह्मन् or शिव is established in his own effulgence—hence called ‘prakāśa’—and inactive. When he starts ‘vimarśa’ or deliberating in himself to create the world, there is a स्पन्द or a throb, which develops into नाद or vibration. This नाद gradually gains in power and then gets concentrated to a बिन्दु or a point. This बिन्दु which contains the शिव-शक्ति principle like a dicotyledonous seed further evolves into शिव and शक्ति principles by the union of which the whole universe comes into being.
As per this description of च्रेअतिओन् given in some तन्त्रस्, all created objects (called ‘artha’) with ‘rūpa,’ shape or form, and ‘nāma’ or name have originated from the primeval नाद, which can now be called ‘Śabda-ब्रह्मन्.’ Hence, it is quite reasonable to assume that every मन्त्र is an aspect of this primeval Word or शब्द-ब्रह्मन् and represents as its अर्थ, a god or a goddess, which again, is a manifestation or emanation of that ब्रह्मन्. In other words, the मन्त्र contains in itself the form and the spirit of the deity, whose मन्त्र it is. This deity is revealed by the proper repetition of the मन्त्र, in course of time.
The तन्त्रस् categorise the mantras as saura (solar) and saumya (lunar). They may be masculine, feminine or neuter. The masculine and the neuter mantras are called ‘mantra’ whereas the feminine mantras are called ‘vidyā’. Mantras ending with huṁ, vaṣaṭ or phaṭ are masculine, those ending with स्वाहा or vauṣaṭ are feminine and those ending with namaḥ are neuter. The तन्त्रस् christen certain monosyllabic mantras like ह्रीṁ or klīṁ as bījamantras or bījākṣaras. Even as a seed evolves in course of time into a mighty tree giving plenty of fruits, a बीजमन्त्र also can give—if properly repeated—the siddhi attributed to it, like the revelation of the deity of that मन्त्र.
A मन्त्र, to be effective, should always be received from a qualified गुरु in a proper way. The तन्त्रस् describe various processes that help in rousing the power of a मन्त्र and make it effective. A few of such processes are: mukha-śodhana (purification of mouth), jihvā-śodhana (purification of the tongue), aśaucabhaṅga (destroying the impurity of the मन्त्र), nidrābhaṅga (awakening the मन्त्र from slumber) and so on.
They also recommend ten सṁस्कारस् or ritual purificatory processes like dīpanī, which consist in repeating the बीज-मन्त्र seven times, preceded and followed by प्रणव (oṁ).
All these have to be learnt directly from a competent teacher and should not be experimented with, by learning them from books.
A theory advocated by the तन्त्रस् regarding the evolution of शब्द or sound, and its corollary, vāk or speech, from the subtle unmanifest state to the fully manifested state is worth mentioning here. When a person speaks, four stages of evolution of speech are involved in it. The speech is first rooted in the mūlādhāracakra as the unmanifest sound. It is then called ‘parāvāk’. When it starts getting awakened and reaches the मणिपूरचक्र at the navel, it has just started showing subtle vibrations. It is now called ‘paśyantī-vāk’.
On its further rising to the अनाहतचक्र in the region of the heart, these vibrations have already assumed definite and clear thought-forms. It is then called ‘madhyamā-vāk’. It now comes out as fully articulated speech, the spoken word, called ‘vaikharī-vāk’.
JAPA
A मन्त्र becomes effective only when its जप is done. That is, it should be repeated a prescribed number of times as per the directions of the गुरु.
Japa is of three types. It is ‘vācika’ or ‘ucca’ when done audibly. It is ‘upāṁśu’ if done in whispering tones. If it is done mentally, it is ‘mānasa’. The last is considered as the most efficacious.
During जप, the counting of the number can be done either by hand or by a जपमाला (rosary). The number recommended can vary. For instance, it can be 10 or 12, 28 or 32 or 108, the last number being the most widely recognised.
A human being is supposed to breathe 21,600 times in a day of 24 hours. Leaving aside half this time for sleep, looking after the needs of the body and contingencies, the breathing during the waking and active state is 10,800 times. Actually the number 108 symbolically represents this 10,800. In other words, a votary is expected to utter the मन्त्र with every breath and the number 108 is a reminder of that ideal.
PURAŚCARAṆA
The तन्त्रस् deal with पुरश्चरण, an important topic closely related to the जप of a मन्त्र. The word literally means ‘performing or carrying (caraṇa) before (puras).’ Various interpretations have, however, been offered. Perfecting of the procedure of the mūlamantra (the basic मन्त्र of a deity) since it has to be practised before the acts in which it is to be employed is called as ‘puraścaraṇa’ by some works. According to others, the sādhana पुरश्चरण is so called because the deity of the aspirant, pleased by his devoted practice, moves (caraṇa) before (puras) him.
Puraścaraṇa has several constituent elements: ध्यान (meditation on the form of the deity), पूजा (ritualistic worship), जप of the मन्त्र, होम (oblations into the duly consecrated fire), तर्पण (satiating the deity with the ceremonial offering of water) and ब्राह्मण-भोजन (feeding ब्राह्मणस् of good conduct). If any of these constituent elements cannot be performed, it can be replaced by more जप of the मन्त्र as specified in the tāntric works.
According to another method, repeating the मन्त्र one thousand times per day for eight days, starting it on a Tuesday and ending it on the subsequent Tuesday is also पुरश्चरण.
Some works recommend the repetition of the मन्त्र 24 lakhs of times, followed by an offering of 24 thousand oblations of pāyasa or pudding into the duly consecrated fire. By this type of पुरश्चरण, the मन्त्र becomes perfected and confers on the sādhaka whatever he desires.
The पुरश्चरण of a मन्त्र on the days of solar or lunar एच्लिप्से, while standing in navel-deep water, is stated to be extremely efficacious.
Certain spots like a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, the bank of a river, a cave or a mountain-top, seashore or the precincts of a temple are recommended as more suitable for the practice of पुरश्चरण.
All tāntric works emphasize that unless the मन्त्र has been received from a qualified गुरु in दीक्षा and the sādhanā is done under his guidance, neither पुरश्चरण nor even जप becomes effective.
PŪJĀ
Pūjā or ritualistic worship of the deity is a very important part of tantra-sādhanā. It forms a part of पुरश्चरण also.
When a respected or a beloved guest arrives in a होउसे, the master of the होउसे receives him warmly and offers him all that makes him comfortable and happy. This is the spirit behind पूजा where the guest is God himself.
In any पूजा, the preliminary processes include सङ्कल्प or religious resolve and ceremonial purification of all the items involved in it as the आसन or seat, the vessels and the flowers. Bhūtāpasaraṇa or driving away all the evil spirits that may obstruct the पूजा is another important item. प्राणायाम or regulation of the मिन्द् through the control of breath, भूतशुद्धि or purifying the elements that compose the body of the worshipper, nyāsas or placement of the fingers of the hand on the different parts of the body with a view to purifying them, ध्यान or meditation are the other important steps.
However, the cardinal part of पूजा is the ‘upacāras’ or ways of ritual service. In the shortest mode of पूजा they are five only: गन्ध (sandal paste), puṣpa (flowers), धूप (incense), dīpa (lighted lamp) and naivedya (food). In more detailed forms they are raised to ten or sixteen or even eighteen. Some of them are: आवाहन (inviting the deity), pādya and अर्घ्य (water for washing feet and hands), स्नान (bath), vastra (cloth), यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread), नमस्कार (obeisance) and visarjana or udvāsana (bidding adieu to the deity).
HOMA
Homa or oblations of prescribed things like ghee into a duly consecrated fire, can be done either independently or as a part of पूजा or even पुरश्चरण. Generally, a यन्त्र or a geometrical drawing representing the deity is drawn as directed, the sacrificial fuel sticks arranged over it and the fire is ceremonially lit. After some preliminary processes of purification, the deity, to appease whom the होम is being done, is invoked into it and the various उपचारस् are offered. After the सङ्कल्प or resolve, in which the purpose and the manner of offering the oblations are stated, the oblations are poured into it with the appropriate मन्त्र. The actual number of oblations can be 8 or 28 or 32 or 108 or even 1008, as stated in the सङ्कल्प. The materials considered fit for offering are: ghee, barley, cooked rice, flower, बिल्व (Aegle marmelos) leaves and a few other prescribed things.
YANTRA
The word ‘yantra’ in its most general sense means an instrument by which anything is accomplished. In worship, it is a diagram drawn or engraved or painted on prescribed materials like metal, stone or paper or even a leaf, that helps one to subdue (yantra = niyantraṇa = subduing) his passions like lust and anger and gain greater concentration.
While a मण्डल, a geometrical figure drawn with coloured powders, can be used for the worship of any deity, a यन्त्र also called ‘cakra’, is specific only to a particular deity. Every deity of the Hindu pantheon has its own यन्त्र. If the deity is the सोउल्, the यन्त्र is its body.
Apart from the geometrical drawing or pattern that is appropriate to the deity, a यन्त्र also contains its मन्त्र, inscribed at the proper place. The presence of the deity is invoked into the यन्त्र by worship, the procedure of which is very similar to that of a प्रतिमा or image. A यन्त्र wherein the deity has been roused by duly worshipping it, can then be used for any purpose—especially for the fulfilment of one’s desires—sanctioned by the tāntric works.
NYĀSAS AND MUDRĀS
Transformation of thought is transformation of being. If the various parts of the sādhaka’s body are touched by his fingers and palms with the appropriate mantras, that will induce the presence of the deity in him, thereby transforming him and making him fit for the ritual or the particular process of sādhanā. This is the general principle behind the nyāsas and mudrās.
The word ‘nyāsa’ comes from the root ‘nyas’ (‘to place’). It is generally done by placing the tips of the fingers and the palm of the right hand on the various parts of the body accompanied by parti-cular mantras.
There are several nyāsas out of which a few—the more common ones—can now be described.
Jīvanyāsa is that by which the sādhaka establishes the इष्टदेवता in the region of the heart and thus becomes one with it.
Vyāpakanyāsa, performed by passing the hands all over the body from top to bottom, helps him to feel the presence of the deity as pervading the whole body.
In मातृकान्यास, which is done with the letters of the alphabet, the various letters are placed mentally in the चक्रस् or psychic centres of the body (antarmātṛkā-न्यास) and also in other limbs outside (bahirmātṛkānyāsa) thereby feeling the competence to know शब्दब्रह्मन् in himself.
In pīṭhanyāsa, the internal seat (pīṭha = seat) in the region of the heart, is made fit for the residence of the deity. Sometimes, the word is interpreted as establishing the various शक्ति-pīṭhas (places of पिल्ग्रिमगे sacred to the देवी or शक्ति, such as Kāmarūpa [in Assam] or Jālandhara [in Haryana]) inside one’s own body in a subtle way.
In ṛṣyādinyāsa, the ṛṣi or the sage, the छन्दस् or the Vedic metre and the devatā or the deity are remembered and homage is paid to them.
In करन्यास and अङ्गन्यास, the fingers of the two hands (kara = hand) and the limbs of the body (aṅga = limb) like the heart and the head, are sanctified to make them fit for worship and meditation.
Like nyāsas, mudrās also find an important place in the tāntric rituals. The word मुद्रा is interpreted as that which pleases the deity and makes its heart melt out of compassion for the votary, and hence grant his desires (mud = pleasure, drav = to melt, rā = to give).
In a technical sense the term ‘mudrā’ has several meanings:
pose of hand as in dance or in पूजा;
posture of the body as in हठयोग;
as one of the five makāras, it means various kinds of grains mixed with ghee.
a woman companion of the tāntric sādhaka.
However, it is used widely in the sense of poses of fingers or of hand or hands in relation to worship and meditation.
Some of the more common mudrās are:
Āvāhanamudrā used to invite and welcome the deity in पूजा.
Kūrmamudrā used in meditation on the deity.
Avaguṇṭhanamudrā and matsyamudrā used in offering ड़ोओद् in पूजा to the deity. So also the grāsamudrā and prāṇādi-pañca-mudrās.
Dhenumudrā, goyonimudrā and nārācamudrā are some of the other, more commonly used, mudrās.
The number of mudrās as given in the tāntric works and even पुराणस्, differs considerably. The number varies from 9 up to 108.
KUṆḌALINĪ AND CAKRAS
Brahman and शक्ति are like the two sides of the same coin. The external world is the च्रेअतिओन् of शक्ति associated with ब्रह्मन्. Inside the bodies of human beings शक्ति takes the form of कुण्डलिनी.
Kuṇḍalinī is the basic energy of the entire human being. It is generally pictured as a coiled serpent (kuṇḍali = serpent) lying asleep at the base of the spinal column, called as ‘ādhāracakra’ or ‘mūlādhāracakra’. When it is roused by proper sādhanās under the guidance of a competent गुरु, it passes through the brahma-nāḍī of the सुषुम्ना canal, pierces through the various चक्रस्, ultimately reaching the सहस्रार, where it gets united with शिव.
According to the works on tantra, there are three nāḍīs (canal-like structures for the flow of prāṇic energy) in the region of the spinal column. In its centre passes the सुषुम्ना and to its right, the पिङ्गला. The iḍā is on the left. Iḍā and पिङ्गला are intertwined over the spinal column. Inside the सुषुम्ना is the vajriṇī nāḍī. Inside it is citriṇī and brahmanādī is the inmost. While in the dormant state, the कुण्डलिनी lies at the bottom of the मूलाधार closing the ब्रह्मनाडी with its mouth.
The चक्रस् are so called since they are circular in shape (cakra = wheel or disc). They are actually psychic centres of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and power, situated in the सूक्ष्मशरीर or the subtle body, corres-ponding to certain parts of the physical body. The आधारचक्र or the मूलाधार is situated at the base of the spine behind the anus. The स्वाधिष्ठान is at the root of the sex-organ. The maṇipūra is at the navel. The anāhata is at the region of the heart. The viśuddha is at the throat. The ājñā is between the eyebrows. The सहस्रार is in the top of the head. These चक्रस् are likened to lotuses, each with a certain number of petals, colour and certain mātṛkās (letters of the alphabet as mantras) inscribed on them. The petals are the nāḍīs or subtle nerve channels, which surround and function through each of these centres.
The table gives the details of चक्रस् at a glance.
These six चक्रस् together are collectively called ‘ṣaṭcakras’ and the piercing act of the कुण्डलिनी is designated as ‘ṣaṭcakrabheda’.
The सहस्रार of thousand petals situated at the top of the head is the seventh चक्र and is the destination of कुण्डलिनी.
When the कुण्डलिनी is roused, the मूलाधार lotus rises up, and opens its petals. After the Kunḍalinī leaves it, it assumes its original position as a bud hanging downwards. This procedure applies to all the other चक्रस् also. After reaching the सहस्रार, the Kunḍalinī comes back to its original place. Repeated practice of the Kuṇḍalinīyoga will result in the flooding of all the चक्रस् with अमृत or nectar of bliss, ultimately resulting in मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
6. Some Allied and Relevant Topics
The tāntric literature encompasses a very vast area of subjects. Differences exist not only on the relative importance of the subjects but also on the subjects themselves. An attempt will now be made to present briefly at least some of the more commonly accepted concepts.
These works present seven types of आचार or modes of sādhanā as follows: Vedācāra, Vaiṣṇavācāra, Śaivācāra, दक्षिणाचार, वामाचार, Siddhāntācāra and Kaulācara. However, these seven are more commonly grouped into two, the दक्षिणाचार and the वामाचार. The words may mean the ‘right-hand path’ and the ‘left-hand path;’ or, the ‘favourable path’ and the ‘path involving vāmā or woman.’
Worship of the deity Dakṣiṇakālikā, following the Vedic modes of worship and sādhanā, as also belief in the varṇāśrama system, characterise the दक्षिणाचार.
Vāmācāra needs some explanation and elaboration. It is called as ‘Cīnācāra’ also, since the sage वसिष्ठ is said to have introduced it after learning it from the बुद्ध in Cīnadeśa (Tibet or China), where it was prevalent. Another name commonly attributed to it is ‘Kaulācāra’ or ‘Kaulamārga’. ‘Kula’ means ‘Śakti’ and the name itself is derived from the fact that the worship of शक्ति is predominant in this system of sādhanā. However, other interpretations are also offered for the word कुल and Kulācāra.
The पञ्चतत्त्वस् or पञ्चमकारस् viz., madya (wine), māṁsa (flesh), matsya (fish), मुद्रा (parched grain) and maithuna (coition) are the most essential parts of this sādhanā system. They are meant for the sādhakas of the vīra-type (heroic type), that too under the strict supervision of a competent गुरु. The vīra-sādhaka is one who has risen to much higher levels of spiritual evolution and hence has great self-control.
However, gross abuse of these five tattvas by the lowest of the sādhakas, of the पशु-type (with unsublimated animal passions) has earned a bad name for the whole system, aver some of the तन्त्रस्. This has led to some of them inventing harmless substitutes like coconut water for madya, garlic for māṁsa or brinjal for matsya and so on; or even give highly symbolic interpretations (for e.g., madya = intoxicating knowledge of God; maithuna = union of the कुण्डलिनी with शिव and so on) to the same. Later writers have strongly condemned these abuses and tried to restore the purity of the system.
A tāntric sādhaka has to rise from the level of the पशु to that of the vīra and then to the दिव्य (divine) state. If a vīra-sādhaka has cultivated the divine virtues by great effort, they are most naturally and effortlessly revealed in the दिव्य-sādhaka.
One who is an adept in the कौलाचार and has reached the summit of realization is called a ‘paramahaṁsa’ and he has transcended all the rules of conduct normally prescribed for the lower sādhakas since he is able to see the divine शक्ति in all.
Another आचार that is often mentioned in the tāntric works is the Samayācāra, which is distinguished from the दक्षिणा-cāra, the वामाचार and कौलाचार. In this tradition, the देवी is called ‘Samayā’ and she personifies the very import of the Vedic tradition. Hence Samayācāra is the conduct in accord with the Vedic tradition and for all practical purposes, can be identified with the Vedācāra listed among the seven ācāras. In this school, शिव and शक्ति are equally important. Stress is laid on the अन्तर्याग or internal worship and the rousing of the कुण्डलिनी through successive stages of upāsanā or meditation. Worship of the श्रीचक्र or Śrīyantra is an important aspect of this school.
The श्रीचक्र is a यन्त्र formed by five inverted triangles and four straight triangles as also diagrams of several petals of lotus, with a dot in the centre and some lines at the extremities. It represents the देवी and the gradual evolution of च्रेअतिओन् from her, associated with शिव.
When the श्रीचक्र is built up in a three-dimensional form, it is called ‘meru.’ Worship of the मेरु is considered even better than that of the यन्त्र.
The Samayācāra is sometimes called the ‘Kādimata’ also. This takes us to another topic connected with the श्रीचक्र. The worship of the श्रीचक्र is invariably associated with श्रीविद्या, initiation into which is a must for any sādhaka of the Samayācāra. ‘Vidyā’ means ‘mantra’. ‘Śrīvidyā’ means the मन्त्र associated with the श्रीचक्र. It is also called ‘pañcadaśākṣarīmantra’ since it contains pañcadaśa or 15 letters. In the most common form, they are distributed into three units of 5 letters, 6 letters and 4 letters. In this, the very first letter of the first unit is ‘ka.’ Hence the Samayācāra which lays great emphasis on the repetition and use of this मन्त्र, is called ‘Kādi-mata’, the school advocating the मन्त्र beginning (= ādi) with ka. The sage अगस्त्य is said to be the promulgator of this school.
As against this, there is the ‘Hādimata,’ the school attributed to लोपामुद्रा (wife of the sage अगस्त्य) which stresses the importance of another pañcadaśākṣarī मन्त्र that begins with the letter ‘ha.’
The difference between the two versions of the pañcadaśākṣarī is in the number of effective letters used. Whereas the former has seven letters, the latter has only five.
A षोडशाक्षरी-मन्त्र is also in vogue where the sixteenth letter (ṣoḍaśa = 16) is ‘śrīṁ,’ the other 15 letters being the same.
The Samaya tradition uses two more words—antaryāga and बहिर्याग. The latter consists of worshipping the श्रीचक्र in the traditional Vedic way, with all the उपचारस् or ingredients. The former is meditation on the unity of the goddess and the श्रीचक्र, the world and the श्रीचक्र, the body and the jīvātman as also the alphabet and the goddess.
One of the strangest, but abominable, tāntric practices mentioned in some of the works is the शवसाधना or the ritual of the corpse. The corpse of a healthy person who has just died is secured, washed and anointed. The sādhaka has to sit upon it and meditate on the देवी at midnight, on a new-मोओन् day. If he survives the terrible experiences, he will attain siddhi or command over every aspect of life.
Some scholars believe that this शवसाधना was a typical and clumsy remnant of a primitive belief or ritual connected with death and revival.
7. Śaktipīṭhas
There are several places of पिल्ग्रिमगे associated with शक्ति or the मोथेर्-goddess. They are called ‘Śaktipīṭhas,’ seats of power (pīṭha = seat), associated with शक्ति. A ritual visit to these places is said to confer great religious merit.
The number of such pīṭhas seems to have grown gradually from 4 to 51 or even 108. However the number seems to have got fixed at 51 in course of time.
There is an interesting paurāṇic legend behind the formation of these शक्तिपीठस्. When सती-दाक्षायणी immolated herself in the sacrificial shed of दक्ष (her ड़थेर्)—since he had humiliated her and her husband Śiva—Śiva carried away her body. Being inconsolable he started roaming about the world, with the dead body on his back. Then विष्णु, at the behest of the gods, started cutting that body by his चक्र or discus so that शिव might overcome his infatuation. Wherever pieces of that body fell, that place became a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे associated with शक्ति, a Śaktipīṭha.
Each of these 51 शक्तिपीठस् is associated with a letter of the alphabet, a part of सती’s body, an aspect of the देवी, a corresponding aspect of शिव, identified with a modern place in the present-day India-Pakistan-Bangladesh region and a special tāntric attainment that can be got by sādhanā there. For instance, the Kāśmīra-पीठ (in the Amarnāth Cave) is associated with the letter ‘u’. It is the place where देवी’s left ear (or neck) fell. महामाया is the goddess and Trisandhyeśvara is the god. Fulfilment of whatever मन्त्र is repeated here, is the attainment.
Some of the other famous शक्तिपीठस् are: Hiṅgula in Baluchistan (now in Pakistan); करवीर in Kolhapur (Maha-rashtra); वाराणसी (in Uttar Pradesh); ज्वालामुखी (in Punjab); कामाख्या (in Assam); जनस्थान (in Nasik, Maharashtra); प्रभास (Girnar hills in Gujarat); Jālandhara (in Haryana); Kanya-kāśrama (in Kanyākumarī temple, Tamil Nadu); उज्जयिनी (in Rudrasāgar, Madhya Pradesh); Kāñcī (in Śivakāñcī, Tamil Nadu), Trisrotā (in West Bengal) and Kālīpīṭha (Kālīghāṭ temple of Calcutta).
8. Conclusion
The तन्त्रस् are a neglected, or even misunderstood, branch of Hindu scriptures. Whether they originated as an offshoot of the Vedic religion, or were a parallel tradition developed by those opposed to the brāhminical hierarchy, or were ‘imported’ from China and Tibet, they have, without doubt, enriched Hindu religion in all its aspects, especially in the field of rituals and spiritual practices. Hence serious attempts should be made to properly edit and publish many of these works which are still lying in the manuscript form in the libraries of institutions and individuals.

tanmātras
(‘only that’)
------------------------------------------
The five primordial elements that manifest from the आत्मन् associated with अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे are called ‘tanmātras’ since each of them contains one quality and only that quality. For instance, the primordial element आकाश has only शब्द (sound or vibration) as its characteristic and hence called ‘śabda-tanmātra.’ The other elements are: sparśa-tanmātra or वायु (air), rūpa-tanmātra or अग्नि (fire), रस-tanmātra or āpas (water), and गन्ध-तन्मात्र or पृथ्वी (earth). These तन्मात्रस् are also called ‘sūkṣma-bhūtas’ (subtle elements) or ‘apañcīkṛta-bhūtas’ (uncompounded elements). Further च्रेअतिओन् takes place out of them, associated, of course, with the आत्मन्.

Tantravārttika
------------------------------------------
The Pūrvamīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि (200 B. C.) has 2700 sūtras spread over 12 chapters containing 60 subsections. The earliest and the most authoritative commentary on it is by शबरस्वामिन् (100 B. C.) and is called Śābarabhāṣya.
Kumārilabhaṭṭa (8th century A. D.) wrote three works in verses on this Śābarabhāṣya, out of which the Tantra-vārttika is the second. It covers the portion 1.2 to the end of chapter 3. It is quite voluminous.
See also KUMĀRILA BHAṬṬA and MĪMĀṀSĀDARŚANA.

Tantrasamuccaya
------------------------------------------
It is a well-known work dealing mainly with temples and temple-rituals. Actually, it is a compendium which has brought together in one place, all the essential aspects of the subject from various authoritative sources.
The author is Nārāyaṇan Nampūtiri (or नम्बूदिरि) belonging to an illustrious होउसे of Nampūtiri ब्राह्मणस् called Cennās. He lived in the 15th Century A. D., the year of birth being A.

.
The work is in 12 paṭalas or chapters and has 1801 stanzas in different metres. शङ्कर, the son of the author, has written a commentary called Vimarśinī.
Two more works, the Devālaya- candrikā and Mānava-vāstu-lakṣaṇa, are also attributed to him.
A brief account of the contents of the work may now be given here:
First Paṭala (137 verses)
Selection of a गुरु; selection of a suitable site for the construction of the temple; Vāstubali rite; depositing the निधिकुम्भ (See NIDHIKUMBHA for details.); laying of the bricks; placing of the foundation stone; selection of suitable granite for the construction.
Second Paṭala (150 verses)
Characteristics of the Prāsāda or the temple proper; its measurements; details of construction; about the idol and its pedestal; types of इदोल्स् and their measurements; balipīṭhas; pañcaprākāras or the five surrounding walls.
Third Paṭala (83 verses)
Purification of the site; sowing of the seeds to test the suitability of the site; preparation of the idol; ceremonies for purifying the temple premises; ceremonial placing of the idol in water and related rituals.
Fourth Paṭala (116 verses)
Purification of the maṇḍapas or temple halls; offering oblations to minor deities; purification of the spot where the kalaśas (ceremonial pots of water) are kept; kindling of the sacred fire; worship of the bed to place the idol horizontally before installing it; bathing the idol with the waters of the kalaśas.
Fifth Paṭala (148 verses)
Purification of the preceptor and spiritually converting his body into a body of fire; ceremonially placing the akṣaras or varṇas (letters of the alphabet) on the various parts of the body of the preceptor; oblations into the sacrificial fire in connection with the ceremony of installation.
Sixth Paṭala (141 verses)
Consecration of the idol; depositing of the precious stones in the hole below the seat of the idol; fixing the idol to the seat with the specially prepared gum-paste called aṣṭabandha; installation of the सप्तमातृकास् (‘seven mothers’); installation of the बलिपीठ and ध्वजस्तम्भ (flag staff); purification of the deity.
Seventh Paṭala (142 verses)
Details of the daily services; meditation of various kinds; worship of the deity with sixteen items (called ṣoḍaśopacāra-पूजा).
Eighth Paṭala (197 verses)
Preparation of kalaśas with 25 articles and water as also their purification; kalaśas for different deities like शिव, दुर्गा, गणपति, सुब्रह्मण्य, शास्ता and शङ्करनारायण.
Ninth Paṭala (240 verses)
Conduct of festivals; erection of the flagstaff; oblations to the bhūtas (spirits) and the deity; propitiation of the Sapta-mātṛkās; putting the deity to sleep; procession of the उत्सवमूर्ति.
Tenth Paṭala (106 verses)
Expiations of various kinds to offset the effects of improper performance of daily rituals; purification of the idol called ‘catuśśuddhi’.
Eleventh Paṭala (124 verses)
Rituals connected with the renovation or reconstruction of the temple structure; of the idol, the pedestal etc., refixing the idol with the aṣṭabandha paste.
Twelfth Paṭala (217 verses)
Miscellaneous topics; additional rituals; hand-poses for rites; specifications for making sacrificial utensils; yantras or diagrams for worship; some mantras of deities and their use.
Though the work contains many details of temple rituals and associated subjects, only a very brief account has been presented here.
